chapterTag.category: AI Math Unit 4 — Probabilistic Machine Learning

body.en: Uncertainty is omnipresent in real-world data. Bayes' Theorem provides the mathematical framework for updating beliefs when observing new evidence, forming the core of Bayesian machine learning and Naive Bayes classifiers.

label.en: ▲ Theorem 4.1 — Bayes' Theorem in Machine Learning

body.en:
For hypothesis (class) \( C \) and observed evidence (features) \( \mathbf{x} \):
\[ P(C | \mathbf{x}) = \frac{P(\mathbf{x} | C) P(C)}{P(\mathbf{x})} \]
Where:
• \( P(C) \) is the Prior probability of class \( C \).
• \( P(\mathbf{x} | C) \) is the Likelihood of observing features \( \mathbf{x} \) given class \( C \).
• \( P(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_k P(\mathbf{x}|C_k)P(C_k) \) is the Marginal probability (Evidence).
• \( P(C | \mathbf{x}) \) is the Posterior probability.

body.en: Proportional Invariance, Linear Structure & Quantitative Modeling: Across Mathematics for Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning, multi-step problems reduce to identifying invariant quantities—constant rates of change \(m = \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\), conservation of total work/mass, or linear system rank conditions. A two-variable linear system \(a_1 x + b_1 y = c_1\), \(a_2 x + b_2 y = c_2\) has a unique intersection if \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} \ne \dfrac{b_1}{b_2}\), no solution (parallel lines) if \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} \ne \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}\), and infinitely many solutions if all three ratios coincide.

body.en:
Why Successive Multipliers & Harmonic Average Speed Work: If a quantity \(Q_0\) undergoes a percentage change \(p\%\) followed by \(q\%\), the compound multiplier is the product of individual scale factors:

\[ Q_{\text{final}} = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\!\left(1 + \frac{q}{100}\right) = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p + q}{100} + \frac{pq}{10000}\right) \]

Notice the cross term \(\dfrac{pq}{10000}\): an increase of \(p\%\) followed by a decrease of \(p\%\) yields \(Q_0\bigl(1 - (p/100)^2\bigr) < Q_0\). Similarly, traveling equal distance \(d\) at speeds \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) takes total time \(T = \frac{d}{v_1} + \frac{d}{v_2}\), so average speed is the harmonic mean \(v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{2d}{d/v_1 + d/v_2} = \dfrac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).
body.ar: برهان النسب المتتالية والسرعة المتوسطة التوافقية: عند زيادة مقدار بنسبة \(p\%\) ثم خفضه بنسبة \(p\%\) يكون الناتج \(Q_0(1 - (p/100)^2) < Q_0\)، والسرعة المتوسطة لرحلتين متساويتين في المسافة هي الوسط التوافقي \(\frac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).

body.en:
An email filter processes emails where \( 20\% \) are spam (\( P(S) = 0.20 \)) and \( 80\% \) are legitimate (\( P(L) = 0.80 \)). The word 'lottery' appears in \( 60\% \) of spam emails (\( P(W|S) = 0.60 \)) and in \( 1\% \) of legitimate emails (\( P(W|L) = 0.01 \)). If an incoming email contains the word 'lottery', what is the probability that it is spam?

Solution:
By Bayes' Theorem:
\[ P(S|W) = \frac{P(W|S)P(S)}{P(W)} \]
Calculate total probability \( P(W) \):
\[ P(W) = P(W|S)P(S) + P(W|L)P(L) = (0.60)(0.20) + (0.01)(0.80) = 0.12 + 0.008 = 0.128 \]
Compute posterior:
\[ P(S|W) = \frac{0.12}{0.128} = \frac{120}{128} = \frac{15}{16} = 0.9375 \].
Despite only 20% of all emails being spam initially, observing the word 'lottery' raises the probability to \( 93.75\% \).
Answer: \( 93.75\% \) (or \( 0.938 \)).

label.en: Worked Example \(B\) — Conditional Probability, Bayes' Rule & Classifiers (Medium Application)
label.ar: مثال محلول B — الاحتمال الشرطي وقاعدة بايز ومصنفات الذكاء الاصطناعي (تطبيق Medium)

body.en:
Problem (Medium): Given \( n = 4 \) independent observations from a normal distribution with sum \( \sum_{i=1}^{4} x_i = 12 \), what is the Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE) \( \hat{\mu}_{\text{MLE}} \)?

Step-by-Step Solution: The log-likelihood \( \ln L(\mu) = -\frac{n}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum (x_i - \mu)^2 \). Setting \( \frac{\partial \ln L}{\partial \mu} = 0 \) yields the sample mean \( \hat{\mu} = \frac{1}{n}\sum x_i = \frac{12}{4} = 3 \).
body.ar:
مسألة (Medium): Given \( n = 4 \) independent observations from a normal distribution with sum \( \sum_{i=1}^{4} x_i = 12 \), what is the Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE) \( \hat{\mu}_{\text{MLE}} \)?

الحل خطوة بخطوة: The log-likelihood \( \ln L(\mu) = -\frac{n}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum (x_i - \mu)^2 \). Setting \( \frac{\partial \ln L}{\partial \mu} = 0 \) yields the sample mean \( \hat{\mu} = \frac{1}{n}\sum x_i = \frac{12}{4} = 3 \).

body.en:
Problem (Hard): A logistic regression model produces a class probability \( p = P(y=1|\mathbf{x}) = 0.40 \). Compute the corresponding log-odds (logit) \( \ln\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) \).

Step-by-Step Solution: Odds are \( \frac{p}{1-p} = \frac{0.40}{0.60} = 0.6667 \). Taking natural logarithm: \( \ln(0.6667) = -0.405 \).

label.en: Worked Example \(D\) — Conditional Probability, Bayes' Rule & Classifiers (Easy Application)
label.ar: مثال محلول D — الاحتمال الشرطي وقاعدة بايز ومصنفات الذكاء الاصطناعي (تطبيق Easy)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): A medical diagnostic test for a rare disease is designed to be highly sensitive and specific. The disease affects \( 1 \) in every \( 1000 \) individuals in the population. The test has a sensitivity of \( 99 \)\% (meaning it correctly identifies \( 99 \)\% of individuals who have the disease) and a specificity of \( 95 \)\% (meaning it correctly identifies \( 95 \)\% of individuals who do not have the disease). If a randomly selected individual from the population tests positive, what is the probability that they actually have the disease?

Step-by-Step Solution: Let D be the event that an individual has the disease, and P be the event that the individual tests positive. We are given the following probabilities: - Prior probability of having the disease: \(P(D) = \frac{1}{1000} = 0.001\) - Prior probability of not having the disease: \(P(D^c) = 1 - P(D) = 1 - 0.001 = 0.999\) - Sensitivity (true positive rate): \(P(P|D) = 0.99\) - Specificity (true negative rate): \(P(P^c|D^c) = 0.95\) From specificity, we can derive the false positive rate: \(P(P|D^c) = 1 - P(P^c|D^c) = 1 - 0.95 = 0.05\). We want to find the probability that an individual actually has the disease given a positive test result, which is $P(D|P)$. We can use Bayes' Theorem: \[P(D|P) = \frac{P(P|D) P(D)}{P(P)}\] To find \(P(P)\), the overall probability of testing positive, we can use the law of total probability: \[P(P) = P(P|D) P(D) + P(P|D^c) P(D^c)\] Substitute the given values: \[P(P) = (0.99)(0.001) + (0.05)(0.999)\] \[P(P) = 0.00099 + 0.04995\] \[P(P) = 0.05094\] Now, substitute \(P(P)\) back into Bayes' Theorem: \[P(D|P) = \frac{(0.99)(0.001)}{0.05094}\] \[P(D|P) = \frac{0.00099}{0.05094}\] \[P(D|P) \approx 0.0194346\] Therefore, the probability that a person who tests positive actually has the disease is approximately \( 0.0194 \), which is closest to \( 0.019 \).

body.en:
1. Adding Successive Percentages or Averaging Speeds Arithmetically: On Mathematics for Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning, a \(20\%\) discount followed by a \(20\%\) increase gives \(0.80 \times 1.20 = 0.96\) (a net \(4\%\) loss, not \(0\%\)). Likewise, average speed for a round trip at \(40\) and \(60\text{ km/h}\) is \(\dfrac{2(40)(60)}{100} = 48\text{ km/h}\), never \(50\text{ km/h}\).

2. Failing to Flip the Inequality Sign When Multiplying/Dividing by a Negative: In \(-5x + 7 \le 12\), dividing by \(-5\) strictly reverses \(\le\) to \(\ge\).

question.en: [Practice 1 · Medium] A spam classification model identifies \( TP = 30 \) genuine spam emails and \( FP = 10 \) legitimate emails falsely flagged as spam. What is the precision of this model?
question.ar: [تدريب 1 · Medium] A spam classification model identifies \( TP = 30 \) genuine spam emails and \( FP = 10 \) legitimate emails falsely flagged as spam. What is the precision of this model?

hints.en: Precision is the fraction of predicted positive instances that are truly positive: \(\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}\).
hints.ar: Precision is the fraction of predicted positive instances that are truly positive: \(\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}\).

solution.en: Precision is the fraction of predicted positive instances that are truly positive: \( \text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} = \frac{30}{30 + 10} = \frac{30}{40} = 75.0\% \).
solution.ar: Precision is the fraction of predicted positive instances that are truly positive: \( \text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} = \frac{30}{30 + 10} = \frac{30}{40} = 75.0\% \).

question.ar: [تدريب 2 · Hard] Compute the Manhattan (\( L_1 \)) norm and Euclidean (\( L_2 \)) norm of the word vector \( \mathbf{w} = [10, -15]^T \).

hints.en: Set up the initial relation: \( L_1 \) norm is the sum of absolute values: \( |10| + |-15| = 25 \).
hints.ar: Set up the initial relation: \( L_1 \) norm is the sum of absolute values: \( |10| + |-15| = 25 \).

question.en: [Practice 3 · Easy] Consider two vectors, \( \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \) and \( \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \). What is the vector representing \( 2\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \)?
question.ar: [تدريب 3 · Easy] Consider two vectors, \( \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \) and \( \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \). What is the vector representing \( 2\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \)?

hints.en: To find the vector \( 2\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \), we first compute \( 2\mathbf{u} \) and then subtract \( \mathbf{v} \) from the result.
hints.ar: To find the vector \( 2\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \), we first compute \( 2\mathbf{u} \) and then subtract \( \mathbf{v} \) from the result.

solution.en:
To find the vector \( 2\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \), we first compute \( 2\mathbf{u} \) and then subtract \( \mathbf{v} \) from the result.

\( 2\mathbf{u} = 2 \times \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \times 3 \\ 2 \times 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} \).

Now, we subtract \( \mathbf{v} \) from \( 2\mathbf{u} \):

\( 2\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 - 1 \\ 8 - (-2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 8 + 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 10 \end{bmatrix} \).

Therefore, the resulting vector is \( \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 10 \end{bmatrix} \).
solution.ar:
To find the vector \( 2\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \), we first compute \( 2\mathbf{u} \) and then subtract \( \mathbf{v} \) from the result.

\( 2\mathbf{u} = 2 \times \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \times 3 \\ 2 \times 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} \).

Now, we subtract \( \mathbf{v} \) from \( 2\mathbf{u} \):

\( 2\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 - 1 \\ 8 - (-2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 8 + 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 10 \end{bmatrix} \).

Therefore, the resulting vector is \( \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 10 \end{bmatrix} \).

question.en: [Practice 4 · Medium] Consider a dataset of \( n \) observations \( (x_i, y_i) \) for \( i = 1, \dots, n \), where \( x_i \) are scalar predictor variables and \( y_i \) are scalar response variables. The ordinary least squares (OLS) estimates for the intercept \( \beta_0 \) and the slope \( \beta_1 \) of the linear model \( y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \epsilon \) are given by \( \hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2} \) and \( \hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x} \). Suppose we have a dataset where \( n = 5 \), \( \sum x_i = 15 \), \( \sum y_i = 30 \), \( \sum x_i^2 = 55 \), \( \sum y_i^2 = 210 \), and \( \sum x_i y_i = 105 \). A new data point \( (x_6, y_6) \) is added to the dataset. If the new regression line that minimizes the sum of squared errors for the \( n+1 = 6 \) points is parallel to the original regression line (i.e., \( \hat{\beta}_1^{\text{new}} = \hat{\beta}_1^{\text{old}} \)), what is the value of \( y_6 \) in terms of \( x_6 \)?

question.en: [Practice 5 · Hard] Consider a dataset of \( n \) data points, where each data point is a vector in \( \mathbb{R}^{D} \). A non-linear dimensionality reduction technique maps these data points to a lower-dimensional space \( \mathbb{R}^{d} \). The mapping function for a single data point \( \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{D} \) is given by \( f(\mathbf{x}) = \phi(\mathbf{x}) \), where \( \phi: \mathbb{R}^{D} \to \mathbb{R}^{d} \) is a function designed to preserve local neighborhood structures. Suppose the mapping \( \phi \) is defined by an explicit feature map \( \phi(\mathbf{x}) = [\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}, \dots, \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}]^T \) where the vector \( \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{10} \) and \( d \) is the dimension of the embedded space. If the goal is to embed these points into a space such that pairwise Euclidean distances are preserved as closely as possible under a specific distortion, and it is found that \( d=15 \) yields optimal results for this mapping under a certain constraint, determine the effective rank of the feature map's image space.
question.ar: [تدريب 5 · Hard] Consider a dataset of \( n \) data points, where each data point is a vector in \( \mathbb{R}^{D} \). A non-linear dimensionality reduction technique maps these data points to a lower-dimensional space \( \mathbb{R}^{d} \). The mapping function for a single data point \( \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{D} \) is given by \( f(\mathbf{x}) = \phi(\mathbf{x}) \), where \( \phi: \mathbb{R}^{D} \to \mathbb{R}^{d} \) is a function designed to preserve local neighborhood structures. Suppose the mapping \( \phi \) is defined by an explicit feature map \( \phi(\mathbf{x}) = [\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}, \dots, \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}]^T \) where the vector \( \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{10} \) and \( d \) is the dimension of the embedded space. If the goal is to embed these points into a space such that pairwise Euclidean distances are preserved as closely as possible under a specific distortion, and it is found that \( d=15 \) yields optimal results for this mapping under a certain constraint, determine the effective rank of the feature map's image space.

solution.en: The feature map is defined as \( \phi(\mathbf{x}) = [\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}, \dots, \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}]^T \), where \( \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{10} \). The term \( \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x} \) is the squared Euclidean norm of \( \mathbf{x} \), denoted as \( \|\mathbf{x}\|^2 \). This is a scalar value. Thus, the mapping \( \phi \) produces a vector where each component is the same scalar value, \( \|\mathbf{x}\|^2 \). Let \( k = \|\mathbf{x}\|^2 \). Then \( \phi(\mathbf{x}) = [k, k, \dots, k]^T \) in \( \mathbb{R}^{d} \). This means that the image of the mapping \( \phi \) is a subspace spanned by a single vector. For example, if \( d=15 \), then \( \phi(\mathbf{x}) = [k, k, \dots, k]^T \) which can be written as \( k \cdot [1, 1, \dots, 1]^T \). The vector \( [1, 1, \dots, 1]^T \) forms a basis for the image space. Therefore, the dimension of the image space, which is equivalent to its rank, is 1, regardless of the value of \( d \) (as long as \( d \ge 1 \)). The problem states that \( d=15 \), but the effective rank of the image of this specific feature map is always 1, as all output vectors lie on a single line passing through the origin.
